WITH ev AS (                           -- a retried event is one event
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (playlist_id, user_id, track_id, action, event_ts)
         event_id, playlist_id, user_id, track_id, action, event_ts
  FROM playlist_events
  ORDER BY playlist_id, user_id, track_id, action, event_ts, event_id
), seq AS (                            -- every event with the one that follows it for the same track
  SELECT ev.*,
         LEAD(action)   OVER w AS next_action,
         LEAD(user_id)  OVER w AS next_user,
         LEAD(event_ts) OVER w AS next_ts
  FROM ev
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY playlist_id, track_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id)
), adds AS (
  SELECT s.playlist_id, s.user_id,
         (s.next_action = 'remove'
          AND s.next_user <> s.user_id
          AND s.next_ts - s.event_ts <= INTERVAL '24 hours') AS removed_by_other
  FROM seq s
  JOIN playlists p ON p.playlist_id = s.playlist_id
  WHERE s.action = 'add'
    AND p.is_collaborative
)
SELECT playlist_id, user_id,
       COUNT(*)                                    AS additions,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE removed_by_other)    AS removed_by_others,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE removed_by_other)::numeric / COUNT(*), 4) AS removed_share
FROM adds
GROUP BY playlist_id, user_id
ORDER BY playlist_id, user_id;

Explanation. Collapse retried rows first (below Very Hard this is a no-op), then give every event the event that follows it for the same playlist and track. Because adds and removes of one track alternate, the event after an addition is either its removal or nothing; pairing by LEAD rather than by a join is what keeps a removal after a re-add from being credited to the first addition. The filter to additions comes after the window function, the collaborative-playlist filter with it. An addition with no next event has NULL next_action, so the boolean is NULL and FILTER (WHERE …) does not count it. The 24-hour test is inclusive; in a UTC session next_ts - event_ts is an exact elapsed interval, and INTERVAL '1 day' compares equal to INTERVAL '24 hours'.

Complexity. One sort for DISTINCT ON, one for the window by (playlist_id, track_id, event_ts, event_id), then a hash aggregate: O(n log n). At scale the window partitions by playlist, which parallelises cleanly; a single huge playlist is a skewed partition but still small in absolute terms.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: no DISTINCT ON or named WINDOW in older code; dedupe with QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY playlist_id, user_id, track_id, action, event_ts ORDER BY event_id) = 1; TIMESTAMP_DIFF(next_ts, event_ts, SECOND) <= 86400; COUNTIF. Snowflake: QUALIFY, DATEDIFF('second', …) (counts boundaries crossed, so prefer TIMESTAMPDIFF on seconds or compare next_ts <= DATEADD(hour, 24, event_ts)), COUNT_IF. Spark SQL: lead(), count_if, unix_timestamp differences. MySQL 8: LEAD works; no FILTER or DISTINCT ON: SUM(CASE …) and ROW_NUMBER(); TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, …).

Edge cases built into the data. A removal by another member exactly 24 hours after the addition (counts) and one at 24 hours and one second (does not); a self-removal within minutes; additions never removed; removals after more than a day. Hard: a track removed by its adder, re-added by another member and removed by a third within 24 hours of the first addition; random re-adds; a non-collaborative playlist edited by its owner. Very Hard: retried rows, including a retried addition whose removal by another member counts.

Common mistakes. Joining each addition to any later removal of the track (credits the re-add's removal to the first addition); filtering to add before LEAD; partitioning by playlist only (the next event is another track's); < instead of <= at 24 hours; counting self-removals; deduplicating after LEAD, or by event_id (the retries have distinct ids); integer division in the share; keeping non-collaborative playlists.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Replay the log per (playlist, track) and keep tracks whose last event is an add; gaps in the log make "still there" uncertain, so reconcile against a periodic snapshot of contents. (2) Order by server receipt for pairing but keep device time for the 24-hour test, or define the window on server time and say so; offline edits can arrive after the window, so the metric needs a lateness bound before it is final. (3) Small denominators: require a minimum number of additions, show counts beside the share, or shrink toward the global rate. (4) Partition by event date and keep yesterday's open additions (no next event yet) as state; each day pairs today's events with that state, and a day's numbers are final 24 hours after its end.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape but pairs additions with any later removal, or counts self-removals. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also handles offline edits, small samples and incremental computation credibly.

Strong signals. Asks how a re-added track is paired before writing SQL; dedupes on content rather than event_id; checks the 24-hour boundary. Red flags. A correlated subquery per addition scanning all later events; treating the current contents of a playlist as recoverable without a full log.

Reference solution (PostgreSQL; {{min_streams}} is the instance's floor, 1 at Medium)

WITH s AS (
  SELECT st.album_id, st.market,
         (st.stream_ts AT TIME ZONE m.tz)::date - a.release_date AS day_no
  FROM streams st
  JOIN markets m ON m.market = st.market
  JOIN albums a  ON a.album_id = st.album_id
)
SELECT album_id, market,
       COUNT(*)                                AS first_week_streams,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE day_no = 0)      AS release_day_streams,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE day_no = 0)::numeric / COUNT(*), 4) AS release_day_share
FROM s
WHERE day_no BETWEEN 0 AND 6
GROUP BY album_id, market
HAVING COUNT(*) >= {{min_streams}}
ORDER BY album_id, market;

Explanation. timestamptz AT TIME ZONE zone gives the wall-clock time in that zone (a timestamp without zone), so its date is the local date, with daylight saving applied for that instant. Date minus date is an integer in PostgreSQL, so the day number is exact and the first week is days 0 to 6 whatever the clocks did. Release day and first week are then filters on one integer. The floor is "at least", applied to first-week streams after filtering.

Complexity. One pass over streams with two small hash joins and a hash aggregate: O(n). At scale the date conversion is per row and cheap; the cost is reading streams, so a pre-aggregate by (album, market, local date) is the natural serving table.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: DATE(stream_ts, m.tz) gives the local date; DATE_DIFF(local_date, release_date, DAY); COUNTIF. Snowflake: CONVERT_TIMEZONE(m.tz, stream_ts)::date; DATEDIFF('day', release_date, local_date); COUNT_IF. Spark SQL: to_date(from_utc_timestamp(stream_ts, tz)) (its timestamps are session-zone instants, so check the session zone is UTC) and datediff(local_date, release_date). MySQL 8: CONVERT_TZ(stream_ts, '+00:00', tz) needs the time zone tables loaded, otherwise it returns NULL; DATEDIFF.

Edge cases built into the data. Streams at local 00:00:00 on release day and at 23:59:59 on day 6 in every market; streams shortly after local midnight and shortly before it, which fall on another UTC date in markets far from UTC (including UTC+5:30). Hard: streams after the first week, including the first second of day 7; one pair exactly at the floor and one a stream short. Very Hard: release weeks containing the European or US clock change, with streams in the last local hour of day 6, which 168 hours from the release instant would miss.

Common mistakes. Taking the date in UTC (or in the session zone); stream_ts::date with a non-UTC session; BETWEEN 0 AND 7; the week as release + INTERVAL '7 days' built from a UTC midnight, or 168 hours from the local midnight; the floor as > instead of >=; applying the floor to all streams instead of first-week streams; integer division.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Bucket by local hour from the same local timestamp; on a fall-back day one local hour occurs twice (keep both, labelled with the offset) and on a spring-forward day one hour does not exist, so the axis has 23 or 25 buckets. (2) Per-listener zones match the listener's experience but make "release day" differ inside a market; per-market zones make the report comparable; whichever is chosen, store it in the definition. (3) Pre-aggregate by (album, market, local date) using each market's zone at write time, or by UTC hour with offsets that are multiples of 15 minutes (UTC hours alone cannot place a +5:30 or +5:45 market's midnight); partition streams by UTC date. (4) Keep a lateness bound (three days here), mark first-week numbers provisional until release + 7 days + the bound, and recompute affected days when late data lands.

Rubric anchors. 2: right aggregation but days in UTC, or the week boundary off by one. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains DST-safe boundaries and the pre-aggregation grain.

Strong signals. Asks which time zone defines release day before writing SQL; compares dates, not hours; mentions the half-hour zone. Red flags. Hard-coding offsets per market (wrong across DST); converting with string manipulation.

WITH counted AS (                      -- this exercise's counting rules
  SELECT p.listener_id, t.artist_id, p.ms_played, p.played_at
  FROM plays p
  JOIN tracks t ON t.track_id = p.track_id
  WHERE p.ms_played >= 30000
    AND NOT p.private_session
    AND p.played_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '{{year}}-01-01 00:00:00+00'
    AND p.played_at <  TIMESTAMPTZ '{{next_year}}-01-01 00:00:00+00'
), per_artist AS (
  SELECT listener_id, artist_id,
         SUM(ms_played)  AS total_ms,
         MIN(played_at)  AS first_play
  FROM counted
  GROUP BY listener_id, artist_id
), ranked AS (
  SELECT per_artist.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY listener_id
                            ORDER BY total_ms DESC, first_play, artist_id) AS artist_rank
  FROM per_artist
)
SELECT listener_id, artist_rank, artist_id,
       ROUND(total_ms / 60000.0, 1) AS minutes
FROM ranked
WHERE artist_rank <= 5
ORDER BY listener_id, artist_rank;

Explanation. Every rule about which plays count is applied once, before aggregation, so the minutes and the tie-break see the same plays: a short or private play neither adds minutes nor counts as a "first play". Aggregating per listener and artist gives the total and the first counted play; ROW_NUMBER over total_ms DESC, first_play, artist_id is fully deterministic and returns exactly five rows. Ranking uses milliseconds; rounding happens only in the output.

Complexity. A scan of plays, a hash join to tracks, a hash aggregate per (listener, artist), and a window sort within each listener's handful of artists: O(n + A log A) for A listener–artist pairs. At hundreds of millions of listeners this parallelises by listener with no global sort.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (…) <= 5; ROUND(total_ms / 60000, 1) returns FLOAT64 (half away from zero, but binary floats can surprise at .x5; use NUMERIC if it matters); TIMESTAMP('{{year}}-01-01') is UTC. Snowflake: QUALIFY; ROUND on a NUMBER is half away from zero. Spark SQL: row_number() in a subquery; round is HALF_UP. MySQL 8: ROW_NUMBER() in a CTE; booleans as private_session = 0.

Edge cases built into the data. Plays of exactly 30 000 ms (count) and 29 999 ms (do not); two artists tied on counted milliseconds for fifth place, where the one played first has the larger artist_id; a short play for the tie loser that would break the tie if counted. Hard: plays at the first and last second of the year (count) and one second either side (do not), large enough to change ranks; private-session plays long enough to enter the top five; a listener with only three artists, plus one artist they only played briefly. Very Hard: the tie loser's very first plays are short and come before the winner's first counted play.

Common mistakes. Filtering short plays after computing the first play; RANK()/DENSE_RANK() (six rows on a tie); breaking ties by artist_id only; ranking on rounded minutes; EXTRACT(YEAR FROM played_at) in a non-UTC session, or BETWEEN including midnight of the next year; ms_played > 30000; LIMIT 5 on the whole result; counting private sessions.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Aggregate per (listener, artist) in a job partitioned by listener hash, keep a bounded top five per listener (a heap or ROW_NUMBER within a partition), validate a sample against an independent computation, and publish atomically before the reveal date. (2) Recompute that listener's card from the remaining history (deletion must propagate to derived data), or hide the card if a recomputation is impossible before display; document the rule. (3) Convert each play to the listener's zone for the year boundary; plays in the first or last hours of the year move between years, so the cut-off must be recorded with the listener's zone at the time. (4) Credit full minutes to each credited artist (artists' totals then exceed the listener's time) or split them; either is defensible if the card's wording matches it.

Rubric anchors. 2: right top five in simple cases but ties or short plays mishandled. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also designs the yearly computation at scale and handles deletions.

Strong signals. Asks whether short plays count for the tie-break; chooses ROW_NUMBER and explains why; uses half-open ranges. Red flags. Non-deterministic order inside ties; treating the summary as a public ranking of listeners.

from bisect import bisect_left


def reorder_moves(old, new):
    # Match copies in order: the k-th copy of a track in old is the k-th copy in new.
    where = {}
    copies = {}
    for i, t in enumerate(old):
        k = copies.get(t, 0)
        copies[t] = k + 1
        where[(t, k)] = i
    copies = {}
    seq, added = [], 0
    for t in new:
        k = copies.get(t, 0)
        copies[t] = k + 1
        i = where.get((t, k))
        if i is None:
            added += 1
        else:
            seq.append(i)
    removed = len(old) - len(seq)
    # Longest increasing subsequence of old positions, by patience sorting.
    tails = []
    for p in seq:
        j = bisect_left(tails, p)
        if j == len(tails):
            tails.append(p)
        else:
            tails[j] = p
    return (removed, added, len(seq) - len(tails))

Explanation. Kept entries that are not moved keep their relative order, so they form an increasing subsequence of their old positions read in new order; every other kept entry must be moved, and moving each of them once is enough (place each in turn next to an entry already in its final relative order). So the fewest moves is kept − LIS. Removals and additions are separate operations and do not affect which kept entries can stay. Copies of one track are matched in order ((track, k) keys), which turns duplicates into distinct labels. Patience sorting: tails[k] is the smallest last element of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1; bisect_left because positions are distinct and the subsequence must be strictly increasing.

Complexity. O(n) for the maps, O(n log n) for the LIS; memory O(n). The timing test has 200 000 entries with half of them swapped: the reference takes about half a second, while the quadratic DP is ~2 × 10¹⁰ steps (the DP alone takes about a second at n = 5 000 in CPython).

Common mistakes. Counting positions that changed; LCS by the O(n²) table; list.index inside a loop (O(n²)); counting additions or removals as moves; bisect_right (harmless here because positions are distinct, but wrong for a non-strict variant; ask them why); matching copies by a dict from track to one position (the second copy overwrites the first); returning a list instead of a tuple is fine, a wrong order of the three numbers is not.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Keep a predecessor array alongside tails to recover one LIS; the entries outside it are the moves; apply them in new order, each placed right after its predecessor in the new list (or at the top). (2) Three-way merge: compute both diffs against the base, apply non-overlapping operations from both, and treat the same track moved to two places, or moved by one and removed by the other, as conflicts resolved by a rule (last writer by server time, or keep both positions out); version vectors per playlist detect concurrency. (3) Most edits touch few entries: sync sends the client's operations instead of recomputing a diff, and the server recomputes a full diff only when clients diverge; or diff in blocks with hashes to find the changed region first.

Rubric anchors. 2: correct answer with O(n²) LIS or LCS. 3: correct O(n log n) with a clear reduction. 4: also recovers the moves and discusses concurrent edits.

Strong signals. Reduces to LIS quickly and proves why n − LIS suffices; tests the reversed and single-move cases. Red flags. Counting changed positions; sorting the new list (destroys the order being measured).

def shortest_completion(plays, album):
    need = set(album)
    seqs = {}
    if plays and len(plays[0]) == 2:                       # (listener, track), in time order
        for listener, track in plays:
            seqs.setdefault(listener, []).append(track)
    else:                                                  # (ts, listener, track[, ms_played])
        kept = [p for p in plays if len(p) < 4 or p[3] >= 30000]
        kept.sort(key=lambda p: p[0])                      # stable: equal ts keep arrival order
        for p in kept:
            seqs.setdefault(p[1], []).append(p[2])
    out = {}
    for listener, seq in seqs.items():
        counts, have, left, best = {}, 0, 0, None
        for right, t in enumerate(seq):
            if t in need:
                counts[t] = counts.get(t, 0) + 1
                if counts[t] == 1:
                    have += 1
            while have == len(need):
                if best is None or right - left + 1 < best[0]:
                    best = (right - left + 1, left)
                u = seq[left]
                if u in need:
                    counts[u] -= 1
                    if counts[u] == 0:
                        have -= 1
                left += 1
        if best is not None:
            out[listener] = best
    return out

Explanation. Each listener's sequence is independent, so group first (sorting by timestamp with Python's stable sort keeps arrival order for equal timestamps; short plays are dropped before grouping so they take no index). Then the classic minimum window: the right pointer adds plays, a count per album track and a counter of distinct album tracks present tell when the window holds the whole album, and the left pointer shrinks it while it still does. Every minimal window is visited at its right end, and recording only strictly shorter windows keeps the earliest start for a length, because right ends are visited in increasing order.

Complexity. O(n log n) for the sort (O(n) at Medium), then O(n) for the windows: each play enters and leaves the window once. Memory O(n). The timing test has 300 000 plays over three listeners with one album track every few thousand plays: the reference runs in about 0.1–0.2 s; scanning forward from every start takes over 3 s on a tenth of the input and is quadratic in the gap between rare plays.

Common mistakes. One sequence for all listeners; a set per window (O(window) per step); recording <= (gives the latest start on ties); sorting by (ts, track), which reorders a listener's equal-ts plays ((ts, listener) is harmless because Python's sort is stable); keeping short plays and skipping them only when counting (they still take indices); returning listeners who never complete with a sentinel instead of leaving them out.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Medians over completers only are biased toward fast completions; report the completion rate alongside, or a survival-style view (share completed within N plays). (2) Streaming: per (listener, album), keep the last position of each album track; when a play arrives, the current shortest window ending now starts at the minimum of those positions, so state is O(album size) per listener–album, and only albums the listener has touched need state. (3) Index album membership track → albums, process each listener's sequence once, and update per-album last-seen positions for the albums of each play; cost is proportional to plays times albums per track, not plays times all albums.

Rubric anchors. 2: correct with a scan per start, or a window with a tie error. 3: correct O(n) window with grouping and the level's ordering and filtering rules. 4: also the streaming formulation and the many-albums restructuring.

Strong signals. Groups per listener first; explains why strictly-shorter updates give the earliest start; drops short plays before indexing. Red flags. Producing per-listener output for a report rather than aggregates; sorting the whole input by track.

def apply_queue(context, ops):
    # Sentinels are tuples, so they can never equal a string entry id.
    HEAD, SPLIT, TAIL = ("head",), ("split",), ("tail",)
    nxt = {HEAD: SPLIT, SPLIT: TAIL}
    prv = {SPLIT: HEAD, TAIL: SPLIT}

    def link_after(a, e):
        b = nxt[a]
        nxt[a] = e
        prv[e] = a
        nxt[e] = b
        prv[b] = e

    def unlink(e):
        a = prv.pop(e)
        b = nxt.pop(e)
        nxt[a] = b
        prv[b] = a

    for e in context:
        link_after(prv[TAIL], e)
    playing = None
    for op in ops:
        kind = op[0]
        if kind == "next":
            link_after(HEAD, op[1])
        elif kind == "add":
            link_after(prv[SPLIT], op[1])         # end of the queued part
        elif kind == "remove":
            if op[1] in prv:                      # still in the queue
                unlink(op[1])
        elif kind == "move":
            e, after = op[1], op[2]
            if e not in prv or after == e or (after is not None and after not in prv):
                continue
            unlink(e)
            link_after(HEAD if after is None else after, e)
        elif kind == "advance":
            first = nxt[HEAD]
            if first is SPLIT:                    # queued part empty: take from the context
                first = nxt[SPLIT]
            if first is TAIL:
                playing = None
            else:
                unlink(first)
                playing = first
    out, e = [], nxt[HEAD]
    while e is not TAIL:
        if e is not SPLIT:
            out.append(e)
        e = nxt[e]
    return (playing, out)

Explanation. Every operation names an entry, so the structure must find an entry and its neighbours in O(1): a doubly linked list stored in two dicts, prv and nxt, keyed by entry id. Three sentinels make every rule an ordinary insert. HEAD is the front, so "play next" and a move with after=None link after it. SPLIT sits between the two parts, so "add to queue" links before it (after prv[SPLIT]). TAIL ends the queue. The two-part rule for moves needs no extra code: linking e right after after puts it on after's side of SPLIT, which is exactly "takes after's part". An entry is in the queue exactly when it is a key of prv, which makes the ignored operations one dict lookup each. advance takes the first real node, stepping over SPLIT when the queued part is empty.

Complexity. O(1) per operation and O(n) to walk the result, so O(C + Q) overall. The timing test (150 000 context entries, 150 000 edits) runs in about 0.5 s in CPython. A Python list with index, insert and pop(0) shifts or compares O(n) elements per edit; measured on 200 000 entries and 200 000 edits, it was still running after 300 s, against 0.7 s for the linked list. A deque helps only at the ends; removes and moves still cost O(n).

Dialect notes. In Java the same design is a HashMap<String, Node> over a hand-written doubly linked list (LinkedHashMap cannot insert in the middle). In C++ std::list plus an unordered_map<string, list::iterator> gives O(1) splices (splice moves an element without copying). In a database, ordered lists are usually stored with a sort key per item (fractional indexes) and read with ORDER BY, which trades O(1) edits for occasional renumbering. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Two "play next" requests (the later plays first); "add" after earlier adds and before the context; "add" with nothing queued; advance taking queued entries first; advance on an empty queue (None); removing a played entry; "add" after the queued part has emptied; removing the only context entry, then adding; (Hard) a context entry moved to the front joining the queued part; a queued entry moved after a context entry joining the context; a move after the last queued entry staying queued; a move to the place it already is; (Very Hard) a move after itself; a move after a removed entry; a move of a played entry; advancing past the end, then queueing again.

Common mistakes. Using a counter of queued entries and positions, which breaks when moves cross the boundary; deciding an entry's part from its id or from where it came from instead of where it now is; two separate lists that cannot move an entry across in O(1); unlinking e before checking that after is valid (the entry vanishes when the move is ignored); treating after == e as "stay"; forgetting that SPLIT is not an entry when walking the result or advancing; list.index in the hot path.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Walk from HEAD to SPLIT for "Next in queue" and on from SPLIT for the context; to show the first 50, walk 50 steps. Counts per part can be kept as counters updated on each link and unlink (a move across SPLIT changes both). (2) Keep the original context order (or a version of it) and apply shuffle as a separate order over context entries; turning shuffle off reorders the context part by the original order and keeps removals and moved entries, by a rule the candidate states. (3) Send the final order with a revision number, and the edit log since the last sync; two devices editing at once is the collaborative-playlist problem (SPT-L2-05) in miniature: a single order of operations, operations by entry id. (4) Materialise the context lazily: keep it as an index into the playlist plus a set of edited entries; a move that names an entry far down forces only that entry (and its neighbours) into the linked structure.

Rubric anchors. 2: a list-based simulation that is correct on small inputs but fails the timing test, or one that gets the part rules wrong after moves. 3: all tests pass with a linked list over dicts. 4: also uses a boundary sentinel and explains why it makes the part rule fall out, states the invariant ("in the queue iff in prv"), and answers the display, shuffle and cross-device follow-ups concretely.

Strong signals. Asks what identifies an entry when a track is queued twice; asks which part a moved entry belongs to before coding. Red flags. "Lists are fast enough in practice" without sizing; positions as identifiers.

SPT-L2-02.html:
Reference solution

from bisect import bisect_right


def pick_highlights(clips, min_gap=0):
    order = sorted(clips, key=lambda c: c[2])          # by end
    ends = [c[2] for c in order]
    # best[i] = best (total, -count) using only the first i clips in end order
    best = [(0, 0)] * (len(order) + 1)
    for i, (_cid, start, _end, score) in enumerate(order):
        j = bisect_right(ends, start - min_gap, 0, i)  # clips ending at or before start - gap
        total, neg = best[j]
        take = (total + score, neg - 1)
        best[i + 1] = take if take > best[i] else best[i]
    total, neg = best[-1]
    return (total, -neg)

Explanation. This is weighted interval scheduling. Sort clips by end time. best[i] is the best selection among the first i clips. Clip i is either left out (best[i]), or taken together with the best selection among clips that end at or before start_i - min_gap. Because clips are sorted by end, those clips form a prefix, found with one bisect_right (the <= boundary: a clip ending exactly at start - min_gap is compatible). Comparing (total, -count) tuples applies both rules at once: higher total first, then fewer clips. The search is limited to hi=i; every clip at position i or later ends after start_i, so none of them could be compatible anyway.

Complexity. O(n log n) for the sort and the binary searches, O(n) memory. The timing test (80 000 clips over four hours, up to 20 minutes long) runs in about 0.1 s in CPython. Walking back from each clip to the last compatible one costs O(n × overlap): about 17 s on 60 000 such clips. Comparing every earlier clip is O(n²), billions of steps.

Dialect notes. In Java or C++ use a sorted array of ends with Arrays.binarySearch adapted to "last ≤ x" or std::upper_bound, and pack (total, -count) into a long (for example total * 2^20 - count) to compare in one step. In SQL this DP does not express well (it needs a recursive CTE with a max over a range per row); a batch job would run it per episode in a UDF. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Touching clips (compatible); one second of overlap; no clips ((0, 0)); the highest-scoring clip not in the best set; earliest-end greedy losing; unsorted input; (Hard) a score tie broken by fewer clips (one long clip versus two halves), a clip scored 0, two clips with the same end; (Very Hard) a gap of exactly min_gap (allowed), one second short (not allowed), and touching clips that are no longer compatible when a gap is required.

Common mistakes. Greedy by score or by earliest end; bisect_left (drops the clip that ends exactly at the boundary) or start instead of start - min_gap; sorting by start and then binary searching ends that are not sorted; maximising the total but ignoring the count, or counting clips scored 0; recursion with lru_cache that hits Python's recursion limit at 80 000; returning the clips' scores as floats.

Follow-up guidance. (1) A length budget makes it a knapsack over intervals: best[i][len], O(n × budget), feasible at 90 seconds with 1-second granularity, or a Lagrangian penalty per second if exactness is not needed. (2) Keep a choice bit per i (taken or not) and walk back from the end; a stated tie rule (for example prefer the selection whose clips start earliest) has to be applied inside the comparison, not after. (3) One task per episode, idempotent, writing reels keyed by episode and scoring version; compare old and new reels on agreed metrics (coverage of the episode, score under both functions, listener sampling outcomes in an experiment) rather than "the new score is higher", which is circular. (4) Snap boundaries to the nearest sentence start and end before the DP; the algorithm is unchanged, but clips may collapse into duplicates, which should be merged keeping the best score.

Rubric anchors. 2: greedy, or a quadratic DP that fails the timing test, or the tie rule missed. 3: all tests pass with sort-by-end plus bisect. 4: also states why the compatible clips form a prefix, gets the gap boundary right first time with the right bisect, and gives a careful answer on the length budget or reconstruction.

Strong signals. Asks whether touching clips overlap; produces a three-clip counterexample to greedy unprompted. Red flags. Trusting the score function's numbers as if they were the goal ("the highest score is best") with no word on how the reel is judged.

SPT-L2-03.html:
Reference solution (the fixed report)

from datetime import date

DAY = 86400


def _window(as_of):
    """The 28 days ending with as_of, as [start, end) in seconds of local time."""
    end = (date.fromisoformat(as_of) - date(1970, 1, 1)).days * DAY + DAY
    return end - 28 * DAY, end


def artist_audience(plays, tracks, artists, as_of):
    start, end = _window(as_of)
    streams = {a: 0 for a in artists}
    listeners = {a: set() for a in artists}
    for p in plays:
        if p["ms"] < 30_000:                              # exactly 30 seconds counts
            continue
        info = tracks[p["track"]]                         # removed tracks still count
        for a in [info["primary"], *info["featured"]]:    # every credited artist
            local = p["ts"] + artists[a] * 60             # the artist's own calendar
            if start <= local < end:
                streams[a] += 1
                listeners[a].add(p["listener"])           # a person, not a device
    return {a: {"streams": streams[a], "listeners": len(listeners[a])} for a in artists}

The planted bugs, their symptoms and their fixes.

  1. Exactly 30 seconds is dropped. if p["ms"] <= 30_000: continue skips a play of exactly 30 000 ms. Symptom: the "test listen of exactly half a minute never shows up" complaint, and a small undercount everywhere. Fix: skip only < 30_000.
  2. Featured artists are not credited. Only info["primary"] is counted. Symptom: a featured artist on a hit sees zero streams and zero listeners for it. Fix: loop over the primary and every featured artist.
  3. Listeners counted per device. The set holds (listener, device) pairs. Symptom: one person on a phone, a laptop and a speaker counts as three listeners. Fix: add the listener id only.
  4. The window is taken in UTC. start <= p["ts"] < end compares UTC seconds with a window that is meant to be in the artist's local calendar. Symptom: an artist at UTC+9 sees the day roll over at 09:00 local time, in the middle of their morning; an artist at UTC−5 loses the evening of as_of. Fix: compare ts + offset * 60, per credited artist, inside the artist loop.
  5. Removed tracks are dropped. The live dict leaves out removed tracks, so their past plays vanish. Symptom: a month of plays disappears when a label takes a track down. Fix: look the track up in tracks regardless of removed.

Each bug has its own check that the other bugs do not affect: a single play of exactly 30 000 ms, a single play of a track with a featured artist, one listener on two devices, a play of a removed track (all at local noon in the middle of the window), and plays around local midnight for artists at UTC+9 and UTC−5 at both ends of the window. The Hard check "one play near midnight falls inside the window for one credited artist and outside it for the other" needs bugs 2 and 4 both fixed, and is a good prompt to discuss why the window check must sit inside the artist loop.

Explanation. The report has four independent rules (what counts, who is credited, which calendar, who is a listener) plus one about data that must not be filtered (removed tracks). The subtle one is the window: once a play is credited to several artists in different time zones, the window check has to be made per artist, not once per play.

Complexity. O(P × A) where A is the number of artists on a track (at most a few), so linear in the plays; memory O(artists + distinct listener-artist pairs). The timing test is 200 000 plays.

Dialect notes. In SQL the same report is a join from plays to a track_artists bridge table (one row per credited artist), a filter ms >= 30000, a window on (ts AT TIME ZONE artist_tz)::date BETWEEN as_of - 27 AND as_of, and COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT listener_id) grouped by artist, with a left join from artists for zeros. A join to a "current catalogue" view reproduces bug 5. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Exactly 30 000 ms and 29 999 ms; a featured artist; one listener on two devices; a removed track; 20:00 UTC on as_of for an artist at UTC+9 (outside); 03:00 UTC the day after for an artist at UTC−5 (inside); the first second of the window's first local day and the second before it; an artist with no plays; (Hard) one play that is inside for one credited artist and outside for another; (Very Hard) the day boundary for an artist at UTC+5:30, one second either side.

Common mistakes. Fixing the featured credit but keeping one window check per play; converting with the listener's time zone instead of the artist's; using zoneinfo names when the data gives offsets; fixing the device bug by counting devices per listener; filtering removed tracks "because they are not in the catalogue"; rewriting the report rather than making minimal fixes.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Decide whether history follows the profile's time zone at the time of each day or the current one, and say so on the report; recomputing with the new zone shifts every day's boundary. (2) Remove the person's plays from the stored daily aggregates and recompute the artist's 28-day numbers; small numbers can make a single departure visible, so reports with very few listeners are best shown with a threshold or rounded (aggregates only). (3) Store per artist and local day a mergeable distinct sketch or, where exact counts are required, a per-day set of listener ids; daily distinct counts cannot be summed because the same listener appears on many days. (4) Credits are versioned; recompute the affected window under the corrected credit and show the change with a note, keeping the old numbers in history.

Rubric anchors. 2: finds two or three bugs; some checks still fail. 3: all five fixed, every check passes, each bug explained with its complaint. 4: also moves the window check inside the artist loop and explains why, adds a check per bug, and answers the distinct-count and deletion follow-ups with a concrete storage plan.

Strong signals. Maps each artist complaint to a bug before touching code; asks whose time zone the window uses. Red flags. "Counting devices is close enough"; dropping removed tracks to "match the catalogue".

SPT-L2-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Registry. feeds (feed_id, url, host, show_id, state active|moved|dead, etag, last_modified, last_hash, next_fetch_at, publish_rate). shows (show_id, canonical_feed_id). A show has one canonical feed and may have aliases (old URLs, duplicates) pointing at it.
  • Scheduler. Each feed's next fetch time comes from its observed publishing rate: feeds that publish daily or weekly are fetched often enough to meet the {{freshness}} target around their usual publishing times; dormant feeds back off to once a day or less. Push notifications, where a host supports them, move a feed's next fetch to now; polling continues as a safety net. A per-host token bucket enforces the agreed rate, and a host's queue is fair across its feeds.
  • Fetching. Conditional GET (If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since); a 304 ends the work. A 200 body is hashed; an unchanged hash ends the work. Errors, timeouts and implausible bodies (an empty feed, a feed a tenth of its usual size) are recorded and do not produce changes.
  • Snapshots and diffs. Each changed feed is parsed into a normalised item list and stored as an immutable version (feed_id, version, fetched_at, hash, items). The change set is computed against the previous good version: new items, changed items, missing items.
  • Episode identity. episodes (episode_id, show_id, …) with an episode_keys (show_id, key_type guid|enclosure|title_date, key, episode_id) table. Matching tries the GUID, then the enclosure URL (normalised), then title plus publication date. A match on a fallback key with a changed GUID is recorded as a re-key, not a new episode, so listener libraries keep their ids.
  • Edits. Metadata changes update the episode with a new revision. A changed enclosure (new audio) creates a new audio version for the same episode id; the audio is fetched, checked (format, duration, loudness or validity checks) and only then made live; plays keep the audio version they used.
  • Removals. A missing item is "missing since version V" first; it is unpublished only after it has been missing from N consecutive good fetches or for a grace period, and never when the feed looks truncated (far fewer items than usual, or the missing items are exactly the oldest ones while the host is known to trim). Creators can also remove episodes explicitly through the creator tools.
  • Moves and duplicates. A feed that declares a new URL, or a second submission whose items match an existing show's episodes on enclosure or title-plus-date above a threshold, becomes an alias; episodes are matched across feeds with the identity table, and the canonical feed switches once the new one is confirmed (verification through the show's owner contact or a token in the feed).
  • Audit and support. Every episode change carries the feed version and rule that caused it. The support view for a show lists recent fetches (status, 304, unchanged, changed), parse errors, and per-episode history with the reason an item was not published (missing audio, invalid enclosure, duplicate, held because of a suspected truncation).

Competing designs to accept. Push-first with polling fallback; a simpler fixed-interval schedule with conditional requests if the candidate sizes it and shows it fits the host limits; storing only diffs instead of full snapshots, if a feed can still be reconstructed for audits; a stream of change events (episode created, updated, unpublished) consumed by catalogue, search and notifications.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Fixed-interval polling of all {{shows}} feeds wasting fetches; one slow host blocking a shared worker pool; very large feeds ({{largest_feed}}) parsed in full on every change; GUID churn duplicating episodes; truncated feeds unpublishing back catalogues; audio replaced in place under listeners; per-host limits breached after an outage when everything is due at once.

Follow-up guidance. (1) The 50-item fetch looks truncated (the missing items are the oldest, and the item count fell sharply): hold, mark missing, change nothing for listeners; the next full fetch clears the marks. (2) Alias the new feed to the show, match episodes by enclosure or title-plus-date into the existing episode ids, record re-keys, and switch the canonical feed after verification; the old feed is polled rarely until it dies. (3) A new audio version with a new duration: listeners halfway through resume by proportion or restart with a note, by a stated rule; analytics attribute plays to the audio version, so completion rates are not mixed across versions. (4) Per-host token buckets with a catch-up queue ordered by staleness and publishing rate; other hosts keep their own buckets, so they are not starved. (5) The audit trail per episode and per fetch; the support view shows the last fetches and the reason for each held or rejected item.

Rubric anchors. 2: poll every feed on a timer, key episodes on GUID only, delete what disappears. 3: adaptive scheduling with conditional requests and host limits, versioned snapshots and diffs, a stable episode id with fallback keys, grace-period removals. 4: also handles truncated feeds and host migrations explicitly, versions audio separately from metadata, and designs the support view from the audit trail.

Strong signals. Separates the catalogue's identity from the feed's identifier first; asks what a truncated feed looks like. Red flags. "Re-import the whole feed and replace the show's episodes"; no thought for the hosts' capacity.

SPT-L2-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Model. playlist (playlist_id, owner, revision), items (playlist_id, item_id, track_id, added_by, added_at, sort_key, removed_at). An item is one appearance of a track; the same track twice is two items.
  • Operations. add(item_id, track_id, after_item_id), remove(item_id), move(item_id, after_item_id), rename, set_collaborative, each with client_op_id, device_id, account_id and base_revision. Operations name items, never positions.
  • Ordering. The server is the single orderer per playlist: it appends accepted operations to a per-playlist log with consecutive revision numbers (a conditional write on the revision or a single writer per playlist partition). client_op_id makes retries idempotent.
  • Rebasing. Because operations refer to item ids, most operations apply unchanged to the latest revision. Rules: a move or remove of an item that no longer exists is a no-op recorded in history ("item already removed by X"); a move after an anchor that was removed resolves to the anchor's nearest surviving predecessor at the time of removal; concurrent moves of the same item are ordered by revision, so the later one wins and both appear in history; duplicate adds of the same track are two items unless the client sent the same client_op_id.
  • Offline. A reconnecting device sends its queued operations with its base_revision. They are applied in its own order after the current head, each rebased as above, unless the device's account lost edit rights before the operation's local time, in which case it is rejected and the device is told. The device then pulls the operations since its base to converge.
  • Ordering keys. The current order is materialised with sort keys (fractional indexes between neighbours) so that reads are an index scan and a move is one row update; keys that grow too long trigger a rebalance written as an ordinary operation.
  • Storage. The operation log is the source of truth; snapshots every N operations (or when the log since the last snapshot exceeds a size) make reads cheap: snapshot plus tail. History = the log, with who and when; restore = an operation that sets the order and membership to the version at revision R, appended as a new revision.
  • Analytics. Events per accepted operation (playlist id, operation type, collaborator count bucket, device type) for aggregate reporting of collaboration; no listening data is joined at the person level.

Competing designs to accept. A sequence CRDT (RGA, Logoot, LSEQ or similar) with peer-to-peer convergence and no central orderer; operational transformation over positions (accept if the candidate shows the transformation rules and why item ids are simpler); last-writer-wins on a whole-list document only for very small playlists with a clear statement of the edits it loses. Each must say how convergence is guaranteed.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Positions instead of ids (offline edits land in the wrong place); clock-based last-writer-wins (a fast clock wins every conflict); a hot playlist at a party exceeding a single writer's throughput with {{collaborators}} editors (batch operations per request, coalesce moves of the same item); unbounded logs without snapshots; sort keys that grow without bound; restore implemented as a rewrite that breaks offline devices' base revisions.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Removes of items still present apply; removes of already-removed items are no-ops; moves are applied in the device's order after the head with anchor resolution; the device pulls 2 000 operations (or a snapshot) to converge, possibly after {{offline_window}}. (2) Both see their own move instantly, then the server's order; the later revision wins; history shows both moves. (3) A restore operation at a new revision; an offline operation based on an earlier revision is rebased onto the restored state like any other (an item absent after the restore makes its move a no-op). (4) Track the length of sort keys; rebalance a range by writing new keys as one operation; clients mid-edit continue because their operations name items, not keys. (5) Counts of operations per playlist and per collaborator bucket per day, active collaborators per playlist, conflict and no-op rates; no per-person listening data.

Rubric anchors. 2: whole-playlist overwrite or positions with last-writer-wins; no history. 3: item ids, a per-playlist operation log with revisions, rebasing rules, snapshots, restore as a new change. 4: also explicit outcomes for every conflict type with history entries, an offline and permission story, sort-key rebalancing, and a convergence argument the interviewer can check.

Strong signals. Separates item from track in the first minute; asks what an offline device knows. Red flags. "Use timestamps to pick the latest version"; locks for editing.

SPT-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Identity. playlists (playlist_id, kind editorial|personalised|user|collaborative, owner_id NULL, generator_id NULL, created_at, deleted_at NULL). Editorial market variants are playlist_variants (playlist_id, market, variant_id) sharing most entries, or one playlist per market linked to a parent; both are fine if "the editorial playlist" can be reported across markets. Personalised playlists are one logical playlist per listener (playlist_id keyed by listener and playlist family), never visible to others.
  • Entries. playlist_entries (entry_id, playlist_id, item_id, added_by, added_at, removed_at NULL, sort_key). The entry id identifies one occurrence, so the same track twice is two entries. Order is a sortable key (fractional or lexicographic keys between neighbours) so a move rewrites one row, not all positions.
  • Edits and versions. playlist_edits (edit_id, playlist_id, version_no, actor_id, op add|remove|move|visibility|rename, entry_id, before_key, after_key, server_ts, client_ts), append-only and ordered by a per-playlist version number assigned by the server (optimistic concurrency: an edit names the version it was based on). playlist_versions (playlist_id, version_no, valid_from, valid_to, source edit|generation_run|editor_publish). Contents at time T = replay edits up to the version valid at T, accelerated by periodic checkpoints (full entry list every N edits or daily).
  • Generated playlists. generation_runs (run_id, generator_version, scheduled_for, status, superseded_by NULL) and the run's output as entry rows tagged with run_id. A re-run is a new run; which run each listener actually received is a fact of delivery (playlist_versions.source = generation_run, run_id), never an overwrite.
  • Plays. Play events carry context_playlist_id; attribution joins on valid_from <= play_started_at < valid_to to get the version, no copy of contents per play. fct_playlist_plays_daily (date, playlist_id, market, version_no, plays, listeners) for editorial playlists; personalised playlists only in aggregates across listeners (per playlist family and day).
  • Follows. playlist_follow_events (playlist_id, listener_id, op, at); fct_playlist_followers_daily derived from events (end-of-day state), with the live count as a cache reconciled nightly.
  • Storage. {{daily_edits}} edit rows a day of tens of bytes each is small; full snapshots per edit (an average playlist of ~50–100 entries rewritten per edit) would be 50–100× larger. Checkpoints plus edits, partitioned by date and clustered by playlist, with older checkpoints thinned beyond a year and everything dropped after {{history_years}} years.
  • Deletion. Deleting an account deletes its user-made playlists, their edits and follow events after the policy's grace period; aggregates already published keep the counts (they contain no identity) and are labelled as such; in collaborative playlists the member's edits are attributed to a "removed member" pseudonym or deleted per policy, while the playlist's current entries remain for the other members.

Competing designs to accept. Snapshots per version with structural sharing (content-addressed entry lists) instead of an edit log. A document store holding the current playlist plus an event log for history. Positions as integers with a rebalancing step, if the cost of moves and the history representation are discussed. Event sourcing with periodic snapshots.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Positions as dense integers (one move rewrites hundreds of rows, history unreadable); snapshot-per-edit storage; client timestamps ordering concurrent edits; generator re-runs overwriting the run listeners saw; follower count as an un-reconciled counter; plays attributed to the current version rather than the one live at play time; duplicates of one track collapsed by using item_id as key.

Incident guidance.

  • Personalised run redone in place: the overwrite destroyed the record of what listeners saw. Contain: stop attribution jobs for the affected window; restore the original run from the raw generation output or backups if available, otherwise mark that period's attribution as unreliable. Guardrail: generation runs immutable with run ids, re-runs as new runs, and delivery records naming the run each listener got ({{personalised_refresh}} refreshes multiply the damage of each overwrite).
  • Snapshot table outgrew the estimate under rapid re-orders: switch to edit log plus checkpoints, coalesce bursts of moves by the same editor into one version for history display while keeping the raw edits, and alert on edits per playlist per hour against the {{daily_edits}} baseline.
  • Remove before add in collaborative history: ordering by client clocks. Order by the server-assigned version number; keep client time only as an attribute; reject an edit based on a stale version and let the client rebase.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Entries with sort keys, versions with validity, reconstruction from the nearest checkpoint plus edits. (2) Server versioning; second edit rebases or conflicts; history shows server order. (3) Item list per run with run id (one row per entry per listener per run); listeners × ~30–50 entries per refresh, retention shorter than editorial history. (4) Interval join on valid_from/valid_to; a play a few seconds after the re-order joins the new version, which is correct if the client fetched it; strong answers note client caching lag. (5) Delete owned playlists and personal edits; aggregates keep counts; collaborative playlist keeps entries, attribution anonymised.

Rubric anchors. 2: one table playlist_id, position, track_id overwritten in place; no history. 3: entries with occurrence ids, versions or edit log, validity intervals for play attribution, follows as events. 4: also concurrency control on collaborative edits, immutable generation runs, a storage estimate with checkpoints, privacy of personalised playlists and deletion handling.

Strong signals. Asks what "version" means for each kind before drawing tables; notices the duplicate-track case. Red flags. Copying the playlist into each play event; positions as dense integers with no move strategy; showing one listener's personalised playlist in analysis at listener level.

SPT-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Items. A shared items (item_id, kind episode|audiobook_edition); kinds never share a measure without a label.
  • Podcasts. shows (show_id, title, publisher_id), seasons (show_id, season_no), episodes (episode_id, show_id, season_no NULL, episode_type full|trailer|bonus, duration_ms, published_at, removed_at NULL).
  • Audiobooks. works (work_id, title, original_language), editions (edition_id, work_id, publisher_id, language, abridged bool, runtime_ms, release_version), series (series_id, title) with series_members (series_id, work_id, position), contributors (contributor_id, name) and credits (contributor_id, work_id NULL, edition_id NULL, role author|narrator|translator|host).
  • Chapters. edition_chapters (edition_id, release_version, chapter_no, title, start_ms, end_ms): ranges over the edition's audio. A re-delivery creates a new release_version; progress is stored as position_ms in the edition, mapped through an alignment table (release_alignment (edition_id, from_version, to_version, from_ms, to_ms, offset_ms)) when the audio itself changed.
  • Rights. availability (item_id, market, channel plan_included|purchasable, valid_from, valid_to).
  • Progress. listening_progress (listener_id, edition_id, position_ms, updated_at, device_id), last-writer-wins by the event time of the latest play, with the history in segments.
  • Allowance ledger. allowance_periods (listener_id, period_start, period_end, granted_ms) reset on the billing date in the listener's time zone; allowance_usage (usage_id, listener_id, period_start, edition_id, listened_ms, occurred_at, reported_at, source online|offline); allowance_topups. Usage is assigned to the period in which listening occurred. Remaining = granted + top-ups − Σ usage; the displayed balance is the online number minus a conservative estimate for devices known to be offline, and is reconciled when they upload.
  • Entitlements. purchases (listener_id, edition_id, purchased_at): permanent, checked before plan availability. Minutes after purchase never create usage lines; minutes before stay where they were.
  • Facts. fct_spoken_listening_daily (date, market, item kind, show_id | work_id, edition_id, minutes_content, minutes_listened) (content minutes = audio covered; listened minutes = wall time, which differ at speed ≠ 1); fct_allowance_monthly (plan, period, listeners, granted_hours, used_hours); "started under allowance then purchased" from usage lines joined to purchases.

Competing designs to accept. Separate catalogues joined by a conformed item dimension. Chapters stored as a JSON array per edition release, if progress is position-based. Allowance as a counter in an online store with the ledger as its audit log, if reconciliation is explicit.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. One audiobooks table (editions collapse, narrators lost); progress stored as chapter id; allowance counted by upload time; purchases checked against plan availability; content-time and listening-time confused; rights without validity intervals.

Incident guidance.

  • Offline usage charged to the new period: usage was attributed by upload time. Re-attribute by occurred_at to the period in which it happened, refund the wrongly charged minutes in the new period, and tell affected listeners on the {{included_hours}}-hour allowance. Guardrail: period assignment by occurrence time with a test for uploads across a reset.
  • Re-delivered edition, resume mid-sentence: positions were carried over unadjusted. Build an alignment between releases (or map by chapter start plus offset within chapter), migrate progress, and keep the old release's chapter table for published reports. Guardrail: a re-delivery with a runtime change cannot go live in any of the {{markets}} markets without an alignment.
  • Purchased titles shown unavailable: entitlement check order was wrong. Purchases first, plan availability second; add a monitor for "purchased but blocked" plays.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Work → editions → credits; hours for the book = sum over its editions' facts. (2) Position-based progress plus alignment; published chapter reports keep their release version. (3) By occurrence time; the listener's balance showed an estimate meanwhile; strong answers say what happens if the old period is already exhausted (allow overage or deduct carefully, stated as a policy). (4) Continue only by purchase or in another plan; analytics record a stop reason "left plan". (5) Ledger totals per plan and month reconcile to the sum of per-listener lines; one check query.

Rubric anchors. 2: one catalogue table with a type column, chapter-based progress, a remaining-hours counter. 3: works/editions/series/contributors, position-based progress, rights intervals, an allowance ledger with occurrence-time attribution, permanent purchases. 4: also re-delivery alignment, offline estimates in the displayed balance, content vs listened minutes, and reconciliation of plan totals.

Strong signals. Asks how allowance is measured before modelling it; separates the work from editions unprompted. Red flags. Charging usage by upload time; purchase entitlements depending on plan rights; mixing episodes and chapters in one unlabelled minutes measure.

SPT-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Profiles. artists (artist_id, display_name, created_at, status active|merged|split_source), artist_id_map (old_artist_id, new_artist_id, event merge|split, effective_at, scope); a merge maps both ids to the survivor; a split creates a new id and maps chosen releases to it from a stated date.
  • Claims and access. artist_claims (artist_id, claimant_org, verified_at, revoked_at), artist_team_members (artist_id, user_id, role admin|editor|reader, granted_at, revoked_at).
  • Credits. track_credits (track_id, artist_id, role primary|featured|songwriter|producer, credit_order, valid_from, valid_to, source_delivery_id). Stream credit goes to primary and featured roles only (this exercise's rule).
  • Streams to artists. From counted streams fct_streams (date, track_id, listener_id, country, city) (internal, not exposed to artists), build fct_artist_daily (date, artist_id, streams, listeners, saves, follows_net) by joining credits valid on the date; streams are additive across tracks, listeners are distinct per artist and day (and recomputed for 7- and 28-day windows, never summed). A listener of a track with a featured artist counts once for each artist.
  • Follows. artist_follow_events (artist_id, listener_id, op follow|unfollow, event_id, occurred_at); current state per (artist, listener) from the latest event by occurred_at with event_id dedupe; fct_artist_followers_daily from end-of-day state. The live number on the profile is a cache, overwritten by the daily recomputation; merges map events through artist_id_map and take the union of distinct followers.
  • Suppression. Breakdown cells below {{min_listeners}} listeners are suppressed; to prevent differencing, suppress at least one complementary cell (or publish an "other" bucket that is itself above threshold), compute country totals and city cells from the same snapshot, and refresh them atomically.
  • Restatement. Merges and splits apply to history by default for profile pages (the artist is one entity), with an artist-facing notice and an audit of numbers before and after; credit corrections apply from their stated date unless the rights holder states otherwise.

Competing designs to accept. Recomputing artist aggregates from scratch daily (simple at the given scale with a columnar engine) rather than incremental maintenance. A graph store for profile identity. Applying merges only forward, if what artists see is explained.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. A single artist_id on the track; summing listeners across tracks or artists; follower counters with out-of-order events; merges done by updating ids in place (no way back); splits without a release mapping; suppression without complementary cells; country and city refreshed at different times.

Incident guidance.

  • Mistaken merge of two artists: reverse it via the id map (the merge was an event, so the pre-merge mapping is known); follows that arrived during the merge week (about {{daily_follows}} a day overall) cannot be attributed with certainty, so keep them on the survivor and offer listeners a re-follow prompt, or attribute by the release the follow came from where that signal exists. Guardrail: merges of profiles with different claimants require review.
  • Credits re-delivery applied to all history: apply from the delivery's effective date instead; restate past numbers only on the rights holder's request with a notice. Monitor large day-over-day changes per artist after deliveries touching {{featured_share}} of a catalogue.
  • Differencing reveals a suppressed cell: totals and breakdowns from different snapshots. Publish both from one snapshot, add complementary suppression, and test that no published cell below {{min_listeners}} can be derived.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Three credit rows; the stream appears once in each of three artists' facts; listeners distinct per artist. (2) Union of distinct followers; past numbers per the stated restatement policy. (3) Split by release mapping; follows stay with the original profile unless a signal exists; tell both artists. (4) City cell = country − Σ other cities unless a complementary cell is suppressed or an "other" bucket is published. (5) Credits by validity date; numbers change from the effective date; an audit table lists changed artist-days.

Rubric anchors. 2: artist column on tracks, follower counter, listeners summed. 3: credit bridge with roles, id map for merges, follow events with derived counts, distinct listeners per artist, threshold suppression. 4: also splits, complementary suppression with one snapshot, restatement policy and team access controls.

Strong signals. Distinguishes additive streams from distinct listeners immediately; treats merges and splits as reversible events. Red flags. Exposing listener-level data to artists; rewriting artist ids in place; suppression that a subtraction defeats.

SPT-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Devices. devices (device_id, device_type, platform, first_seen_at), device_app_versions (device_id, app_version, valid_from); accounts are on events, so shared devices need no owner.
  • Raw events. playback_events (event_id, device_id, account_id, session_id, seq_no, event_type start|progress|pause|resume|seek|skip|stop|transfer_out|transfer_in|remote_command, item_id, position_ms, client_ts, received_at, private_session, offline bool, controller_device_id NULL), append-only, partitioned by received date. Dedupe on (device_id, seq_no) as well as event_id, because a resend can mint new event ids.
  • Event time. Order within a device by seq_no; estimate the device's clock offset from received_at for online events (median of received_at − client_ts per device and day) and correct client_ts; offline events keep corrected client time with an "uncertain" flag.
  • Segments. playback_segments (segment_id, account_id, device_id, item_id, started_at, ended_at, start_position_ms, end_position_ms, private_session, offline, session_id): built per device by closing a segment on pause, stop, skip, seek, transfer or a progress gap. Only the player emits segments; remote commands go to remote_commands (command_id, controller_device_id, target_device_id, command, at) and never create plays.
  • Sessions. playback_sessions (session_id, account_id, private bool, started_at, ended_at): the private flag lives on the session, and a transfer carries the session id, so the new device inherits it. Personalisation and social consumers read through a view that filters private = false, with a test that runs on every release.
  • Facts. fct_listening_daily (date, device_type, item_kind, online|offline, minutes, plays, listeners), fct_handoffs_monthly (month, from_type, to_type, handoffs), offline share. Offline plays are attributed by occurrence date; late arrivals after a close go to a restatement table and a published adjustment, not a silent rewrite.
  • Access. Each listener's own history is served from their own segments; every other consumer reads aggregates; artists receive counts only.

Competing designs to accept. Stream processing that builds segments in near real time with a late-data window plus a daily batch rebuild for late offline uploads. A session-centric model where segments are children of sessions. Using server receive time only (with clear limits for offline plays).

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Ordering by client clocks; counting plays on the controller and the player; private flag on the device rather than the session; offline plays counted on upload day; resends deduped only by event id; progress events spanning midnight split into two plays.

Incident guidance.

  • Controller phones emitting play events: duplicate plays on speakers. Contain by rolling back the release and excluding events from that app version where controller_device_id is set; restate affected days for the {{device_mix}} mix; guardrail: a contract test that controller devices produce only remote commands, and a monitor on plays per active device.
  • Weeks of offline plays after {{offline_days}} days: by design these attribute to when they occurred; publish a restatement of the closed month with the delta per device type, or a stated policy of late adjustments in the current month, and show both numbers' provenance.
  • Private flag lost after handoff: the flag lived on the device. Move it to the session carried on transfer; purge the leaked plays from personalisation inputs and recompute affected outputs; add a release test for transfers in private sessions.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Phone segment, transfer events, speaker segment(s) with controller commands, pause closes a segment, car segment after transfer. (2) On the session, enforced by a filtered view at the consumer boundary, plus a release test and a periodic audit query. (3) Restate or adjust, per stated policy; reports say which. (4) Event time and day attribution skew; fix with seq_no ordering plus offset estimation. (5) Incremental segment building keyed by device with a watermark and a late window; segments spanning midnight are cut at the day boundary for daily facts while the segment stays one entity.

Rubric anchors. 2: one events table queried directly, client time, plays counted wherever an event appears. 3: raw → segments → facts, player vs controller, dedupe, offline by occurrence, private flag carried. 4: also clock-offset correction, resend handling by sequence number, restatement policy, and enforcement of the private flag at consumer boundaries.

Strong signals. Separates player from controller without being asked; puts the private flag on the session. Red flags. Trusting device clocks; offline plays counted on upload day; any consumer other than the listener seeing a listener's history.

SPT-L3-05.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL; {{tol_ms}} is the instance's tolerance in milliseconds)

WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT s.*,
         LEAD(s.segment_id) OVER (PARTITION BY s.listener_id
                                  ORDER BY s.started_at, s.segment_id) AS next_segment_id
  FROM playback_segments s
), pairs AS (
  SELECT a.listener_id,
         da.device_type AS from_device_type,
         db.device_type AS to_device_type,
         to_char(b.started_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC', 'YYYY-MM') AS month
  FROM ordered a
  JOIN playback_segments b ON b.segment_id = a.next_segment_id
  JOIN devices da ON da.device_id = a.device_id
  JOIN devices db ON db.device_id = b.device_id
  WHERE b.device_id <> a.device_id
    AND b.item_id = a.item_id
    AND b.started_at >= a.ended_at
    AND b.started_at <= a.ended_at + INTERVAL '10 seconds'
    AND ABS(b.start_position_ms - a.end_position_ms) <= {{tol_ms}}
    AND NOT a.private_session
    AND NOT b.private_session
)
SELECT month, from_device_type, to_device_type,
       COUNT(*) AS handoffs,
       COUNT(DISTINCT listener_id) AS listeners
FROM pairs
GROUP BY month, from_device_type, to_device_type
ORDER BY month, from_device_type, to_device_type;

Explanation. "The next segment" is a window function: LEAD over each listener's segments ordered by started_at with segment_id as the tie-break gives exactly one candidate per segment. Joining that candidate back gives both rows; every condition is then a plain predicate. The private-session filter is applied to the pair, after LEAD, because a private segment still sits between two public ones. Device ids are compared (two phones are two devices); device types are only reported. The month comes from B, the segment in which playback continued.

Complexity. One sort (or an index scan) by (listener_id, started_at, segment_id) for the window, then hash joins to the next segment and the small devices table, and a hash aggregate. Linear in segments after the sort; the self-join over all later segments is quadratic per listener and wrong besides.

Dialect notes. Snowflake and BigQuery support LEAD with the same frame; they can also return the next row's columns directly (LEAD(device_id) …, LEAD(started_at) …), avoiding the join back. Month text: TO_CHAR(ts, 'YYYY-MM') in Snowflake, FORMAT_TIMESTAMP('%Y-%m', ts, 'UTC') in BigQuery, date_format(ts, 'yyyy-MM') in Spark SQL, DATE_FORMAT(ts, '%Y-%m') in MySQL 8. Interval arithmetic: DATEADD(second, 10, ts) (Snowflake), TIMESTAMP_ADD(ts, INTERVAL 10 SECOND) (BigQuery), ts + INTERVAL 10 SECONDS (Spark), ts + INTERVAL 10 SECOND (MySQL). NOT a.private_session works on a BOOLEAN column in Snowflake, BigQuery and Spark; in MySQL the flag is usually TINYINT, so write a.private_session = 0. None of these variants is executed here.

Edge cases built into the data. A gap of exactly 10 seconds (counts) and of 11 seconds (does not); a position difference of exactly the tolerance (counts) and of the tolerance plus 1 ms (does not); a restart far behind the previous end position (fails only because of ABS); two devices of the same type (counts as type → same type); a handoff whose A ended before midnight on the first of a month and whose B started after it (counts in the new month); a different item started on another device near the same position (not a handoff); a same-device resume (not a handoff); a handoff into a private session (excluded). Hard adds a brief same-device resume between A and the other device (only the resume → other device step counts) and occasional private segments. Very Hard adds public → private → public across three devices within 10 seconds: no handoff is reported, but removing private segments first fabricates one.

Common mistakes. Exclusive boundaries on the gap or the position; counting same-device resumes; comparing device types instead of device ids; not comparing the item; dating by the segment that ended; no position check, or no ABS; including private segments; (Hard+) matching any later segment instead of the next; (Very Hard) filtering private segments before LEAD. Each has a diagnostic.

Follow-up guidance. (1) PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM b.started_at - a.ended_at)); it needs a sort per group, so at volume use an approximate percentile or a histogram of whole seconds (only 11 possible values here, so an exact histogram is cheap). (2) Denominator from all segments grouped by month and device type with a LEFT JOIN of handoffs; decide whether private segments are in the denominator and say so. (3) Widening to "next item in the queue" would need queue state and invites false positives from ordinary track changes; keep it a separate metric. (4) Process per day with the last segment of each listener from the previous day carried over (a one-row overlap per listener), or compute on segments partitioned by day plus a small boundary window; the month is assigned from B so a month boundary needs no special case beyond that overlap.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape but a self-join over all later segments, or device types compared, or a boundary exclusive. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains why private filtering must follow LEAD, handles clock skew in the discussion, and describes incremental computation across day and month boundaries.

Strong signals. Reaches for LEAD with a tie-break unprompted; asks whether private segments still count as "next". Red flags. SELECT DISTINCT to hide duplicate matches from a self-join; comparing timestamps as text; dropping the tie-break so equal start times order arbitrarily.

Incident guidance.

  • Car clock a few seconds slow: B appeared to start before A ended and failed A.ended_at <= B.started_at. Strong answers correct device time with a per-device offset estimated from server receive times before building segments, or allow a small negative gap explicitly and label it; they also notice the drop in one device type's handoffs as the signal.
  • Positions in seconds from one release: a units contract break. Detect with range checks per device type and app version (positions far smaller than durations), quarantine and fix the affected rows by app version, and add a schema contract with units in the field name.
